resultsSummary.question: During evidence acquisition of a suspect SATA drive, which mechanism ensures that the media remains uncorrupted and forensically sound?

options.text: Executing an unbuffered dd copy directly in single-user mode
Employing a hardware or firmware-based write-blocker
Remounting the filesystem as read-only via standard OS mount
Applying NTFS journaling rollback to stabilize clusters

resultsSummary.explanation: A write blocker guarantees that the storage controller blocks any write or metadata update commands, preserving the bitstream integrity of the original evidence.

resultsSummary.question: In NTFS, what is the significance of the $MFT (Master File Table) record size and resident files?

options.text: Each record is 4096 bytes; files smaller than 4KB are automatically encrypted
Each record is 1024 bytes; small files under ~700 bytes can live directly within the MFT record itself
Each record is 512 bytes; resident files cannot have alternate data streams ($DATA)
Each record is variable; resident files are stored only in unallocated cluster space

resultsSummary.explanation: NTFS MFT records are typically 1024 bytes. When file content fits within the standard record along with attributes (resident file, usually < 700 bytes), no cluster outside the MFT is allocated.

resultsSummary.question: Which volatile artifact is commonly parsed to discover injected DLLs, unlinked VAD trees, and hollowed processes in a Windows memory dump?

options.text: Shimcache / AppCompatCache
Virtual Address Descriptors (VAD) and malfind heuristics
Amcache.hve transaction logs
Prefetch file hash headers

resultsSummary.explanation: The Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) tree records memory allocations. Tools like Volatility parse VAD nodes with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE permissions to detect code injection and process hollowing.

resultsSummary.question: What artifact allows an investigator to detect 'Timestomping' on an NTFS partition?

options.text: Comparing $STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamps against $FILE_NAME timestamps
Checking the hardware BIOS real-time clock battery log
Reviewing the Windows Update orchestrator event 1074
Verifying the volume GUID in the BCD store

resultsSummary.explanation: Timestomping utilities commonly alter the easily accessible $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute timestamps ($SI), but frequently fail to modify the corresponding $FILE_NAME attribute ($FN) timestamps, exposing the discrepancy.

resultsSummary.question: An attacker used DNS tunneling for data exfiltration. Which metric in DNS query logs most strongly indicates active tunneling?

options.text: Frequent standard PTR queries for RFC 1918 private addresses
Abnormally high entropy and length in TXT/A subdomains queries sent to a single authoritative name server
High volumes of DNS reply packets returning NXDOMAIN responses
Standard DNSSEC RRSET verification timeouts on TCP port 53

resultsSummary.explanation: DNS tunneling encodes binary/text payloads into high-entropy, long subdomain strings (e.g., base32/hex chunks) queried against attacker-controlled name servers.

resultsSummary.question: Which registry key tracks recently executed GUI applications along with their run counts and last execution timestamps, encoded via ROT13?

options.text: UserAssist (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist)
RunMRU (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU)
AppPaths (HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\App Paths)
ShellFolders (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders)

resultsSummary.explanation: UserAssist subkeys store ROT13-encoded values recording executable names, execution count, and the 64-bit FILETIME of last launch.

resultsSummary.question: What is the primary forensic value of the Windows Prefetch directory (C:\Windows\Prefetch)?

options.text: Proves an application was executed, with execution timestamps, run count, and referenced file/directory handles
Stores full decrypted copies of all clipboard buffers at time of crash
Holds real-time network sockets opened by each process during boot
Contains SHA-256 signatures validated against Microsoft SmartScreen

resultsSummary.explanation: Prefetch files (.pf) are created by the Cache Manager to speed up app loading. Forensically, they confirm execution, last run times, run count, and file dependencies accessed in the first 10 seconds of launch.

resultsSummary.question: If an investigator calculates an MD5 hash and a SHA-256 hash of an E01 image and compares it to the original physical drive acquisition log:

options.text: The E01 file hash will match the physical drive hash exactly byte-for-byte
The internal stored verification hash inside the E01 metadata must match the acquisition hash, even if the raw E01 container hash differs
E01 files do not support cryptographic hashing, requiring raw DD format
Any difference in hashing algorithm automatically invalidates evidence under Daubert standards

resultsSummary.explanation: Expert Witness Format (E01) encapsulates metadata, compression, and header information. The hash of the .E01 container file differs from the raw drive, but the embedded evidence hash recorded in the E01 metadata matches the original raw drive acquisition.

resultsSummary.question: An analyst inspects an artifact with extension '.jpg'. The first 4 bytes are '4D 5A 90 00'. What does this reveal?

options.text: The file is a corrupted JFIF/JPEG image missing its SOI marker (FF D8)
The file is a disguised Portable Executable (PE / EXE / DLL) masquerading as an image
The file is an encrypted BitLocker recovery volume header
The file is a standard PKZIP archive container

resultsSummary.explanation: 4D 5A ('MZ' - Mark Zbikowski) is the unmistakable DOS MZ header for Windows PE binaries (executables and DLLs), proving the file is an executable disguised with a .jpg extension.

resultsSummary.question: In the Windows Security Event Log, which Event ID indicates that a new process has been created (crucial for tracking process execution chains)?

options.text: Event ID 4624
Event ID 4672
Event ID 4688
Event ID 1102

resultsSummary.explanation: Event ID 4688 logs process creation (including parent process ID and command-line arguments when command line auditing is enabled). 4624 is logon, 4672 is special privileges assigned, and 1102 is audit log cleared.
